blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 3 (Cells and Subcellular Organelles), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, compare, label and describe a structure, give examples), as one 4-mark part or in 1+3 / 2+2 sub-parts. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Cells perform all the fundamental activities of life. Explain how cells show movement, nutrition, respiration, excretion, homeostasis, growth and reproduction. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Movement: cells can move; sperm cells move with their flagella, white blood cells travel through the bloodstream to fight infections, and organelles move inside cells.

Nutrition: cells obtain nutrients from their environment to produce energy, build cellular structures and drive biochemical reactions.

Respiration: cells generate energy by breaking glucose to release ATP, the energy currency that powers cellular activities.

Excretion: cells remove waste products through diffusion and active transport, preventing toxic buildup.

Homeostasis: cells keep a stable internal environment by regulating the movement of substances across their membranes.

Growth: cells grow by taking in nutrients and converting them into cellular components.

Reproduction: cells reproduce by mitosis (identical daughter cells for growth and repair) and meiosis (gametes for sexual reproduction).

book_ref.quote: Cells perform all the fundamental activities that characterize living organisms

blocks.prompt: 2 Trace the history of the cell theory from Robert Hooke to Louis Pasteur. (i) Describe the observations of Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Lamarck and Brown. (ii) Describe the contributions of Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow and Pasteur and state the three points of the cell theory. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Early observations:
• 1665, Robert Hooke (English) examined a thin slice of cork of oak tree, and pieces of stem and root, and saw "many little boxes". He concluded that plant parts were made of compartments and named them "cellulae".
• 1673, Anton van Leeuwenhoek (Dutch) made a better microscope and observed living cells in pond water, which he called animalcules.
• 1809, Jean Baptiste de-Lamarck (French) also observed cells in parts of animals and plants.
• 1831, Robert Brown (British botanist) discovered the nucleus in the cell.

(ii) Forming the theory:
• 1838, Matthias Schleiden (German botanist) concluded that all plants are composed of cells; the next year Theodor Schwann (German zoologist) concluded the same for animals.
• Rudolf Virchow (German physician) observed that all cells come from other cells (1855; the book's 1885 is a misprint).
• 1862, Louis Pasteur provided the experimental proof of this idea.
Cell theory: (1) all living organisms are composed of one or more cells; (2) cells are the basic units of structure and function in an organism; (3) cells come only from the division of pre-existing cells.

book_ref.quote: At the beginning of 17th century, many scientists began the use of microscopes

blocks.prompt: 3 Answer the following about microscopes. (i) Define magnification and resolution of a microscope. (ii) Describe how a light microscope forms an image, and give its magnification, resolving power and limitations. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Magnification is a microscope's ability to enlarge the image of an object, shown by the symbol X (a 10X lens makes a 1 µm object appear 10 µm); total magnification = product of the magnifications of all lenses. Resolution is the ability to distinguish between two points that are close together on an object; the greater the resolution, the finer the detail.

(ii) In a light microscope, light passes through the object and then through two glass lenses: one lens produces an enlarged image and the second magnifies it more, forming an enlarged clear image in the viewer's eye.
• Magnification: 1500X (about 1500 times).
• Resolving power: 0.2 µm (1 µm = 1/1000 mm); it cannot distinguish objects smaller than 0.2 µm.
• Limitations: it can view living organisms, but cells are generally transparent, so their components are not distinguishable unless coloured with special stains, and staining usually kills the cells.

book_ref.quote: One lens produces an enlarged image of the object and the second lens magnifies the image more

blocks.prompt: 4 Describe the electron microscope and its two types used by biologists. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Electron microscope: a beam of electrons passes through the object, and magnetic lenses focus the beam on a screen or photographic film to make a much enlarged image. Its resolving power is much greater than the light microscope: it can clearly show objects as small as 0.2 nm (1 nm = 1/1000,000 mm). It cannot be used for living material because of the methods needed to prepare the specimens.

1. Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM): used to view the internal structure of the cell. It transmits a beam of electrons through a very thin specimen and can magnify objects up to 250,000 times.

2. Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM): used to study the details of surfaces of cells or other objects. The surface is coated with metal; when the electron beam hits the metal it is reflected and makes an enlarged image. SEMs can magnify up to 100,000 times.

book_ref.quote: Biologists use two types of electron microscopes

blocks.prompt: 5 Answer the following about the plant cell wall. (i) What are plasmodesmata? How are they formed and why are they important? (ii) Describe the functions of the cell wall. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Plasmodesmata (singular, plasmodesma) are small channels that directly connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring plant cells. They penetrate both the primary and secondary cell walls. They are formed during cell division when parts of the endoplasmic reticulum of the parent cell get trapped in the new cell wall. They allow certain molecules to pass directly from one cell to another, so they are important in cellular communication.

(ii) Functions of the cell wall:
• Provides rigidity to the cell for structural and mechanical support.
• Maintains cell shape and the direction of cell growth, and ultimately the architecture of the plant.
• Prevents expansion when water enters the cell.
• Protects against pathogens and the environment.
• Acts as a store of carbohydrates for the plant.

book_ref.quote: Plasmodesmata penetrate both the primary and secondary cell walls

blocks.prompt: 6 Describe the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane, explaining the arrangement of phospholipids, cholesterol and proteins in it. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The fluid mosaic model, proposed by S.J. Singer and Garth Nicolson in 1972, describes the dynamic nature of the plasma membrane.

Phospholipid bilayer: the basic foundation is a lipid bilayer made of phospholipids. Each phospholipid has a phosphate group at one end; it is hydrophilic (water-loving) at the phosphate end and hydrophobic (water-fearing) along its tail of C-H chains. In the bilayer the hydrophobic tails point inwards and the hydrophilic phosphate groups face outwards, toward the cytoplasm or the extracellular environment. The hydrophobic interior repels water-soluble molecules.

Cholesterol: in eukaryotes, cholesterol molecules are wedged into the phospholipid bilayer and keep the membrane fluid at low temperatures.

Proteins: a collection of proteins float within the lipid bilayer, and some simply adhere to its surfaces; their positioning is related to the cytoskeleton. They act as channels and transporters, attach the membrane to the cytoskeleton, act as receptors and enzymes. Proteins and lipids on the outer surface carry sugar chains (glycoproteins and glycolipids, the glycocalyx) which serve as identification marks.

book_ref.quote: According to the fluid mosaic model, the basic foundation of plasma membrane is a lipid bilayer

blocks.prompt: 7 Describe the techniques used to study the structure of the plasma membrane. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
• Transmission Electron Microscopy: reveals detailed structures of the lipid bilayer and associated proteins.
• Scanning Electron Microscopy: examines the surface topology of cells and membranes.
• Confocal Microscopy: uses laser scanning and fluorescence to create sharp, detailed images of the cell membrane.
• Total Internal Reflection Fluorescence Microscopy: gives high-resolution images of the membrane and its interactions with the cytoskeleton and other components.
• Atomic Force Microscopy: provides topographical images of the membrane at high resolution.
• X-ray Crystallography: determines the atomic structure of membrane proteins.
• Lipidomics: comprehensive analysis of membrane lipids using techniques like mass spectrometry.
• Fluorescence Recovery After Photobleaching: studies the mobility of membrane proteins and lipids by bleaching a fluorescently labelled region with a laser and observing the recovery of fluorescence as unbleached molecules move in.

book_ref.quote: Total Internal Reflection Fluorescence Microscopy is used for high-resolution images of the membrane

blocks.prompt: 8 The nucleolus makes ribosomes. (i) Describe the structure of the nucleolus and its formation. (ii) Explain how eukaryotic ribosomes are produced in the nucleolus and used for protein synthesis. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) The nucleolus is a prominent, darkly stained structure in the nucleoplasm; there may be one or two in a nucleus. It is formed at certain sites of chromosomes called Nucleolus Organizer Regions (NORs), whose DNA encodes ribosomal RNA (rRNA). It consists of granular and fibrillar components and DNA: the granules are ribosomal subunits already formed; the fibrils are the raw materials, i.e. rRNA molecules and associated proteins. Cells producing much protein have a large nucleolus; it disappears at the onset of mitosis and a new one forms from the NORs after division.

(ii) Ribosomal proteins enter the nucleolus and combine with rRNA strands to make two subunits, one small (40S) and one large (60S). The subunits leave the nucleus through the nuclear pores. In the cytoplasm both subunits combine (80S ribosome) for protein synthesis: mRNA provides the instructions taken from DNA and tRNA brings amino acids; the finished chain of amino acids is released. When protein synthesis is not being done, the two subunits separate.

book_ref.quote: Eukaryote ribosomes are produced and assembled in the nucleolus

blocks.prompt: 9 Mitochondria and chloroplasts are thought to have come from prokaryotes. Explain the evidence given in the chapter and the hypothesis about the origin of mitochondria. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Evidence:
• A mitochondrion has its own circular DNA, similar to the DNA of prokaryotes, all kinds of RNA and 70S ribosomes (the ribosome type of prokaryotes).
• Ribosomes inside mitochondria and chloroplasts differ in size and makeup from cytoplasmic ribosomes and are more like those of prokaryotes.
• Both mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA and replicate (grow and reproduce) independently of the cell and its nucleus.
These features are an exception to the cell theory and suggest that these organelles may have originated from free-living prokaryotic cells.

Hypothesis about mitochondria: millions of years ago, small free-living prokaryotes were engulfed, but not consumed, by larger prokaryotes. Over time the two developed a symbiotic relationship: the larger organism provided the smaller with ample nutrients, and the smaller provided ATP molecules to the larger one.

book_ref.quote: Like mitochondria, chloroplasts also contain their own DNA and are able to grow and reproduce independently

blocks.prompt: 10 Describe the structure of a chloroplast and explain how it carries out photosynthesis. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Photosynthesis, the making of food by converting light energy into chemical energy, is carried out in chloroplasts. All green parts of plants contain them, but most photosynthesis occurs in leaves (about one-half million chloroplasts per square millimetre of leaf surface).

Structure:
• Envelope: the ellipsoid chloroplast is enclosed by two membranes with an intermembrane space between them; the outer membrane is much more permeable than the inner.
• Stroma: semi-fluid inside the inner membrane, containing dissolved enzymes; it makes up most of the volume.
• Thylakoids: inner membranes fuse along their edges to form disk-shaped compartments; stacks of thylakoids are grana (a chloroplast may have a hundred or more grana, each with a few to several thylakoids).
• Lamellae: non-green compartments connecting two grana.
• Pigments chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b absorb light; the chloroplast also has its own DNA and reproduces independently.

Working: light is absorbed by chlorophyll in the thylakoid disks; the chlorophyll emits electrons and ATPs are formed. Using these ATPs, in the stroma, low-energy carbon dioxide is transformed into a high-energy compound like glucose.

book_ref.quote: The ellipsoid-shaped chloroplast is enclosed by two membranes

blocks.prompt: 11 Lysosomes are digestive compartments of the cell. (i) What are lysosomal storage diseases? Describe two examples. (ii) Explain the role of lysosomes in selective cell death. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) In lysosomal storage diseases the patient lacks one of the hydrolytic enzymes of the lysosome. The abnormal lysosome fills with indigestible substances that interfere with cellular functions.
• Pompe's disease: the lysosome lacks a glycogen-digesting enzyme, so harmful amounts of glycogen accumulate in liver cells.
• Tay-Sachs disease: an essential lipid-digesting enzyme is missing. Lipids accumulate in the nerve cells of the brain, damaging the nervous system and causing mental retardation and death in early childhood.

(ii) Lysosomes also eliminate whole cells. Selective cell death is a mechanism used by multicellular organisms in development. For example, when a tadpole develops into a frog, the cells of the tail are destroyed by lysosomal enzymes. Many brain cells also die during development; this directed suicide is accomplished by rupture of the lysosomes in the cells being eliminated.

book_ref.quote: The abnormal lysosome fills with indigestible substances, which interfere with cellular functions

blocks.prompt: 12 Describe peroxisomes: their enzymes, functions and the disorder caused by their defects. How are glyoxysomes related to them? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Peroxisomes are single-membrane bounded organelles of all eukaryotic cells, discovered by Christian de Duve, who also discovered lysosomes.

Enzymes and functions:
• Many enzymes are oxidative, carrying out oxidation (removal of electrons and hydrogens); they mainly rid the cell of toxic substances.
• Peroxisomes in liver cells detoxify alcohol and other harmful compounds by oxidation.
• Some contain catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide (a common by-product of metabolism) into water and oxygen: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂.

Disorder: defects cause metabolic disorders; the most serious is Zellweger syndrome, with absent or reduced peroxisomes. It is congenital, has no cure or effective treatment and usually causes death within the first year of life.

Glyoxysomes are similar to peroxisomes but found only in plant cells. Their enzymes convert lipids into carbohydrates; they are most abundant in lipid-rich seeds (castor beans, soyabeans), where during germination they convert stored lipids into carbohydrates that give energy for germination.

book_ref.quote: Many of these enzymes are oxidative that carry out oxidation

blocks.prompt: 13 Describe the structure of the central vacuole of a plant cell and explain its roles in the plant. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Structure: vacuoles are fluid-filled, single-membrane bounded sacs. Cells have many small vacuoles; when a plant cell matures they fuse to form a single large central vacuole, which takes up most of the cell's space (80 percent or more). It is enclosed by a membrane called the tonoplast, and the material inside, the cell sap, differs markedly from the surrounding cytoplasm. (Vacuoles of animal cells are much smaller and mainly store or transport materials temporarily.)

Roles:
• Structural support: with enough water the central vacuoles swell, creating high turgor pressure; this makes the cell rigid and, with the cell wall, maintains the structural integrity of the plant.
• Storage, waste disposal, protection and growth; some stored materials are useful to humans (opium, rubber, garlic flavouring).
• Pigments stored in vacuoles give certain flowers their colours, attracting bees and other pollinators.
• Vacuoles release molecules poisonous to insects and animals, discouraging them from eating the plant.

book_ref.quote: The central vacuole in plant cells plays an important structural role for the plant

blocks.prompt: 14 Describe the structure of eukaryotic cilia and flagella, including the axoneme and the basal body. How do prokaryotic flagella differ? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Cilia and flagella are thin, tail-like locomotor appendages protruding from certain cells. Cilia are short and usually numerous; flagella are longer and fewer. (In humans, cilia line the trachea and sweep mucus and dirt out of the breathing tubes.)

Axoneme: the core of a eukaryotic cilium or flagellum. It contains two central microtubules surrounded by an outer ring of nine doublet microtubules (the "9 + 2" structure). Dynein molecules around its circumference bridge the gaps between adjacent doublets. A plasma membrane surrounds the entire axoneme.

Basal body: the organising centre at the base of the cilium. It has the same basic structure as the outer ring of the axoneme, but each of its nine outer sets has three microtubules (triplets) instead of a doublet. The basal body is actually a centriole (centrioles are hollow cylinders of nine triplets of microtubules).

Prokaryotic flagella have a completely different structure: they are not membrane bounded, are built from repeating units of the protein flagellin and do not contain microtubule triplets.

book_ref.quote: At the base of the cilium its organising centre, called basal body, is present

blocks.prompt: 15 Describe the structure of a generalized prokaryotic cell. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Bacteria and archaea are made of prokaryotic cells, which are much simpler than eukaryotic cells.
• Size: most are 2 to 8 µm long, about one-tenth of a typical eukaryotic cell.
• Nucleoid: there is no nucleus; the much less extensive DNA lies in a more-or-less central region called the nucleoid.
• Cytoplasm: one unit with no internal support structures; membrane-bounded organelles (ER, mitochondria, chloroplasts, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, peroxisomes) are absent.
• Ribosomes: present but smaller, 70S, with 30S and 50S subunits, all scattered freely in the cytoplasm.
• Plasma membrane surrounded by a cell wall of peptidoglycan (a single large polymer of amino acids and sugar), not cellulose.
• In bacteria the wall may be surrounded by a capsule, and there may be extensions for attachment called pili (singular pilus).
• Flagella made of repeating units of the protein flagellin, without microtubule triplets.
• Division: no mitosis or meiosis; the cell divides by direct division (binary fission).

book_ref.quote: Prokaryotic cells are much simpler than eukaryotic ones

blocks.prompt: 16 Define cell signalling. Describe its three steps. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Cell signalling is the ability of cells to respond to stimuli from their environment by producing cellular responses; it involves transmission of signals between cells through a series of molecular events.

1. Signal reception: signalling begins when a signal molecule (ligand) binds to a receptor of the target cell. Receptors are typically proteins embedded in the cell membrane but can also be inside the cell. Each receptor is specific to a particular ligand.

2. Signal transduction: on binding the ligand, the receptor undergoes a conformational change that activates an intracellular signalling pathway. A series of interactions and modifications forms a signalling cascade that amplifies the signal. Small molecules such as cAMP (cyclic AMP), calcium ions and inositol triphosphate (IP₃) act as second messengers, carrying the signal from the receptor to target molecules inside the cell.

3. Cellular response: the pathway often changes gene expression, turning genes on or off. Results include cell growth, division, differentiation or apoptosis (programmed cell death), and changes in metabolism, enzyme activity or the opening and closing of ion channels.

book_ref.quote: Once the receptor binds to the ligand, it undergoes a conformational change

blocks.prompt: 17 What is facilitated diffusion? Describe the two main types of transport proteins involved in it, with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Facilitated diffusion: some molecules are taken into or out of cells with the help of transport proteins in the plasma membrane. When a transport protein helps a substance move down its concentration gradient (higher to lower concentration), the process is facilitated diffusion. No energy is used, so it is passive transport. Its rate depends on how many transport-protein molecules are available in the membrane.

1. Channel proteins: form hydrophilic channels across the membrane that let specific molecules or ions pass. They can be gated or non-gated; gated channels open or close in response to stimuli such as voltage changes, ligand binding or mechanical stress. Examples: ion channels (for Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻) and aquaporins (rapid transport of water).

2. Carrier proteins (transporters): bind the specific molecule they transport, undergo a conformational change and move it across the membrane. They are highly specific and can become saturated, so there is a maximum rate of transport when all carriers are occupied. Examples: glucose transporters and amino acid transporters.

book_ref.quote: When a transport protein helps a substance to move it down its concentration gradient

blocks.prompt: 18 Water moves across membranes by osmosis. (i) Define osmosis and explain the terms hypertonic, hypotonic and isotonic. (ii) What is reverse osmosis and how does it differ from natural osmosis? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Osmosis is the diffusion of water molecules across a cell membrane from an area of higher (water) concentration to lower concentration. It needs no energy, so it is the passive transport of water. It occurs through a selectively permeable membrane, which lets water pass while restricting many solutes. Its direction depends on solute concentrations on the two sides: water always moves from the hypotonic to the hypertonic solution. Osmosis maintains cell turgor in plants and balances water content; aquaporins speed up water transport.
Tonicity is the relative concentration of solutes: hypertonic solutions have more solute, hypotonic solutions less solute, and isotonic solutions equal concentrations.

(ii) Reverse osmosis is a technology for purifying water. Natural osmosis moves water from lower to higher solute concentration; reverse osmosis applies external pressure to push water through a semi-permeable membrane from higher to lower solute concentration. This filters out dissolved salts and impurities, giving clean drinking water; it is used in water treatment plants, desalination facilities and household purifiers.

book_ref.quote: Osmosis occurs through selectively permeable membrane, which allows water to pass while restricting many solutes

blocks.prompt: 19 Define active transport. Describe active transport through carrier proteins, endocytosis and exocytosis. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Active transport is the movement of substances across the plasma membrane from lower to higher concentration with the expenditure of energy.

1. Through carrier proteins: carrier (transport) proteins use energy to move molecules against the concentration gradient. Example: the sodium-potassium pump of nerve cells. In a resting nerve cell it spends ATP to keep K⁺ high and Na⁺ low inside, by moving Na⁺ to the outside and K⁺ to the inside.

2. Endocytosis: bulky materials are moved into the cell. A portion of the plasma membrane invaginates, the outside material is taken into the invagination, its ends seal and a small vesicle forms, which detaches and moves into the cytoplasm. Forms: phagocytosis (solid material) and pinocytosis (liquids as droplets). In receptor-mediated endocytosis, specific receptor proteins pick up material, e.g. liver cells take up LDLs (carrying cholesterol) from the blood.

3. Exocytosis: bulky material is exported. It is packed inside a membrane to form a vesicle, which moves to the plasma membrane, fuses with it and releases its contents into the extracellular environment.

book_ref.quote: Following types of active transport occur through plasma membrane

blocks.prompt: 20 Stem cells have great medical potential. (i) Describe the uses of stem cells in medicine and research. (ii) Why do adult stem cells involve less ethical controversy than embryonic stem cells, and what are their drawbacks? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Uses of stem cells:
• Regenerative medicine: stem cells can repair or replace damaged tissues and organs, so they are used for spinal cord injuries, type 1 diabetes, Parkinson's disease and heart disease.
• Drug testing and development: by differentiating stem cells into specific cell types, researchers create models of human diseases for more accurate testing of drug effects, reducing reliance on animal models.
• Personalized medicine: stem cells can be derived from a patient's own cells, reducing the risk of immune rejection and giving more effective and safer therapies.

(ii) Embryonic stem cells come from the inner cell mass of blastocysts, so their use raises ethical concerns about using human embryos, besides risks of teratoma formation and immune rejection. Adult stem cells are found in tissues such as bone marrow, fat and blood, so no embryo is used; when taken from the patient's own tissues the risk of immune rejection is also lower. Drawbacks: they are multipotent, with limited differentiation potential (only cell types related to their tissue of origin), and they are harder to isolate and culture.

book_ref.quote: Stem cells have the potential to repair or replace damaged tissues and organs
